Gold futures rose Friday, but the rally failed. What I’m watching next week
body: The $3,879 area is an immediate test, while $3,820-$3,850 could become an important battleground if selling resumes.

Gold futures finished Friday, November 13, at $3,887.6 on the continuous COMEX chart. Although the session ended slightly higher, the journey tells a less encouraging story for bulls. Buyers initially pushed prices above $3,920, only to lose almost their entire advance. That makes the next recovery attempt particularly interesting.
The Friday futures session opened Thursday evening at $3,883.3 and climbed to $3,927.2. By Friday morning, however, gold had fallen to $3,871.1 before recovering modestly into the close.
Approximately 90% of the initial $43.9 rally was surrendered.

When buyers push prices higher but cannot maintain their progress, it can indicate weakening bullish conviction. Traders who interpreted the early advance as a sign of strength may have been disappointed.
Both Thursday and Friday saw gold futures trade below the October 30 low of $3,879.3, yet both sessions closed above it.
That suggests sellers have not established lasting control beneath this reference level. It is a possible sign of stabilization, although certainly not confirmation of a bullish reversal.
Gold struggled to sustain trading above this area on Friday. Recovering it and holding above it on the hourly chart would be an encouraging first step for bulls.
A sustained recovery through this region would suggest buyers are regaining some control. Beyond that, $3,989-$4,006 becomes a more meaningful recovery area.
Failure to defend this region, especially with daily closes below it, would weaken the tentative stabilization argument and bring Thursday's $3,856.7 low back into focus.
This is my broader downside watch zone, immediately below the latest weekly low.

If gold tests this area, I believe bulls need to show a convincing defense. Otherwise, sustained weakness through the zone could encourage bears to become more aggressive, interpreting the failure as evidence that buyers are losing control.
Importantly, this is an opinion about how the market might respond, not a prediction that gold must reach this zone or that sellers will necessarily accelerate.
Gold futures lost approximately 4.7% over the week on the continuous chart, finishing close to their weekly low. The $3,856.7 low also represents a new 20-week low.

news.title: investingLive Americas market news wrap: Hawkish Fed worries ebb after PPI
body: The PPI numbers were something of a respite to the drumbeat of inflation worries as the main numbers were 0.1 pp below estimates. That was generally balanced by non-stop Fed talk on inflation, with Goolsbee saying the recent CPI number was "borderline alarming" and others striking a similar tone. BofA was out with a note to change its Fed call to three consecutive hikes in Dec, Jan and March. All that helped to keep a bid in the dollar, which finisehd at hte best levels of the day. The euro continues to test the Liberation Day lows.

In equity markets, the closing levels don't tell the story as the selling was heavily concentrated in AI and chip names. AMD led the re-think with an 8% loss and pre-market gains for Nvidia reversed. The thinking is that the US is going to draw a hard line against China sales and remote use, curbing the market and -- ultimately -- allowing China to build its own chip companies. Outside of that, breadth was positive and there were some bright spots like Meta with a 2.8% gain. Next week features a heavy does of retail earnings so that will be a good check on the consumer.

Iran news was generally quiet but there was talk of a strike on US radar facilities in Bahrain. Iran claims it was hit, the US claims the drones were shot down. There was little or nothing on negotiations, so it appears we've reached a standstill and the oil market wasn't overly volatile.

news.title: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
body: Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.

The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks.

"Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.

The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.

Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.

Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed.

Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.
The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

news.title: Earnings week ahead: Nvidia without Jensen, Anthropic’s IPO, and the consumer meets a hiking Fed
body: Earnings season is supposed to be over. Instead, next week might be the most important of the quarter for the macro view.

Nvidia reports days after losing its founder. Anthropic prices what could be the largest equity deal ever. And every major US retailer reports into a rate-hike cycle. October CPI came in hot at 0.4% headline and 0.3% core, a December hike is fully priced with a 12% chance of 50 bps, 10-year yields sit at 5.13% and Brent is above $98.
The AI trade gets two tests in 48 hours: Nvidia’s guide on Tuesday and Anthropic’s pricing on Wednesday. Then the consumer gets its turn.

A quiet start, with China doing the talking. XPeng, Baidu, H World and KE Holdings cover Chinese autos, ad spending, hotels and housing in one morning. KE is the one I’d watch. It is the cleanest real-time read on whether property transactions have found a floor.
Tyson Foods is the US name to watch. Protein prices are where households feel inflation after the gas pump. Listen for trade-down from beef to chicken and anything on restaurant demand.

Home Depot reports before the open, with consensus at $3.86 on $42.72 billion in revenue. The numbers matter less than the commentary. Housing turnover was already frozen when the Fed was cutting and now mortgage rates are heading the wrong way. The question for Ted Decker is whether big-ticket projects are getting pushed out again and what pros are saying about backlogs.
Retail sales hit at 8:30 am ET, so you get the company view and the government view within the same hour.

Klarna is an underrated macro report. Buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are an early warning on the low-end consumer. Disney parks and Viking tell you whether the high end is still spending on experiences.

Then Nvidia after the close. The Street is at roughly $109.2 billion against the company’s $108 billion guide, and it’s Colette Kress’s first report as interim CEO. The quarter was in the bag before Jensen left, so the print itself is not the risk, the guide is. Nvidia is the single best indicator of the AI capex cycle, and that cycle has been a meaningful slice of US growth. If there’s any wobble in the outlook, it’s not just a Nvidia problem, moreover, we could find out that the China book is a big part of sales and that could now be gone.

Target, TJX and Lowe’s before the open, and the contrast is the story. TJX is a market darling and can still win when consumers trade down. Target loses when they stop buying things they don’t need. If TJX beats and Target misses again, that is a consumer that’s still spending but increasingly picky, the same pattern as the last two years.
Lowe’s is the cross-check on Home Depot, with more DIY and less pro.
ZIM is worth a look for container rates and what the Middle East is doing to shipping lanes. Tencent gives you China gaming and advertising.

After the close, Helmerich & Payne is the one for the oil market. With crude near $100, are US shale producers finally adding rigs? If not, the supply response isn’t coming, and that matters for the inflation outlook. Palo Alto Networks is a read on the boom in AI security. Copa covers Latin American travel demand and jet fuel costs.

The bigger event that night isn’t an earnings report. Anthropic prices its IPO, with 825 million shares marketed at $70 to $78. The top of the range raises $64.35 billion, and with the private placement the total hits $90.4 billion. That values the company at up to $1.4 trillion fully diluted, down from the $2 trillion floated in September.
